entities.name: Juan José Alvarado
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Juan Bautista Alvarado (1809–1882) was a California-born politician who served as Governor of Alta California under Mexican rule (1836–1842) — making him one of the few native Californio leaders to achieve the governorship through political skill rather than appointment from Mexico City. His governorship coincided with a critical period in California's history: the collapse of the Franciscan mission system, the redistribution of mission lands to the great ranchos, and the increasing penetration of foreign American and Russian traders that foreshadowed California's eventual incorporation into the United States.

Born in Monterey to a Californio family with deep roots in Alta California, Alvarado was educated at the Monterey Presidio and built a political career in the provincial diputación — the territorial legislature. His 1836 revolt against the appointed Mexican governor established him as the effective ruler of California, which he governed for six years.

His administration saw the secularization of the Franciscan missions — converting the missions from church-controlled institutions to secular towns and redistributing their vast lands to Californio ranching families.

He lived to see California's American conquest and the Gold Rush transform the world he had governed.
